name: Iron

lead: Iron is needed for oxygen transport and many enzymes. People with diffuse hair shedding, fatigue or pallor take it hoping to bring hair back to normal density, and some take it for under-eye shadows.

Follicle cells divide quickly and depend on iron-containing enzymes, and low stores are thought to push follicles early into the resting phase, causing telogen effluvium. Clinicians commonly check ferritin and haemoglobin in unexplained shedding, and correcting a confirmed deficiency is the accepted treatment for deficiency-related shedding. No randomised trial in the available research tests iron for hair outcomes.

paras: Oral iron is usually taken as a daily tablet after a blood test such as ferritin confirms low stores, often with vitamin C and apart from calcium. Shedding recovers over months as stores refill.

Oral iron commonly causes constipation, nausea and dark stools. Excess iron accumulates in people with haemochromatosis and promotes oxidative damage, and accidental overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under six. Guidance advises testing first.

social.title: New iron nanomaterial wipes out cancer cells without harming healthy tissue

angle.text: Iron is supplemented by people with diffuse hair shedding or pale skin who have low iron. Follicles depend on iron-containing enzymes, so restoring low stores lets hair cycle normally and reduces shedding. Benefits with normal iron levels are untested.

lead: Iron is an essential mineral (chemical symbol Fe) needed for oxygen transport in haemoglobin and myoglobin, for energy production, for DNA synthesis and for many enzymes [1]. About 65 to 70 percent of the roughly 3 to 4 grams of iron in the human body is bound in haemoglobin [1]. In nutrition and appearance discussions the word refers to dietary iron and oral or intravenous iron supplements rather than the metal itself, which is the subject of the general encyclopedia article [2].

Iron deficiency, with or without anaemia, is described as the most prevalent nutritional deficiency worldwide and is especially common in women who menstruate, children, adolescents and pregnant women [3][1][4]. In looksmaxxing, iron comes up mainly in connection with diffuse hair shedding, fatigue and skin pallor. Clinicians commonly check ferritin and haemoglobin in people with unexplained shedding, and correcting a confirmed deficiency is the accepted treatment for deficiency-related shedding; no randomised trial in the available research record tests iron specifically for hair outcomes, and supplementing people with normal iron stores is not supported by hair-specific evidence.

Iron can also cause harm. Oral iron commonly causes gastrointestinal effects, excess iron accumulates in people with haemochromatosis and promotes oxidative damage, and accidental overdose of iron-containing products is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under six, according to product labelling [1][5].

paras: Iron is given orally or intravenously to prevent and treat iron deficiency and iron-deficiency anaemia, including in pregnancy; a US prescription iron-folic acid product, for example, is labelled for iron-deficiency and folate-deficiency anaemia and for prevention and treatment of iron deficiency in pregnancy [5]. A 2025 JAMA review addresses diagnosis and treatment of iron deficiency in adults [6]. Intravenous iron is used when oral therapy is not tolerated or ineffective and in some chronic conditions; a 2025 meta-analysis of six trials (7,175 patients) of intravenous iron in heart failure with iron deficiency reported lower rates of the composite of recurrent heart-failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death at 12 months than placebo [7].

Hair follicle cells divide rapidly and rely on iron-containing enzymes such as ribonucleotide reductase. Dermatology guidance commonly describes low iron stores as one possible contributor to telogen effluvium, in which more follicles than usual shift into the resting phase, and iron status is often measured when evaluating diffuse shedding. Appearance communities discuss iron mainly as one item in a nutrient check alongside vitamin D, zinc and thyroid function. Cited hair-specific trial evidence is limited; the evidence base for correcting deficiency rests largely on clinical consensus and the general literature on iron deficiency.

Oral iron raises haemoglobin and ferritin in people who are deficient. Comparisons between formulations are an active research area: a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials compared ferrous bisglycinate, an amino-acid chelate, with other iron supplements for effects on haemoglobin and ferritin in adults and children [8], and a randomised trial in pregnancy reported that 25 mg of iron as ferrous bisglycinate was as effective as 50 mg of iron as ferrous sulfate for preventing deficiency and anaemia [9]. A randomised trial in iron-depleted young women found that oral iron supplements raise hepcidin, the hormone that limits iron uptake, and reduce absorption from subsequent doses, which has been cited in discussion of daily versus alternate dosing [10][11].

For anaemia in pregnancy, randomised trials have compared a single-dose intravenous iron approach with oral iron [12][13]. A 2025 meta-analysis examined the optimal dose and duration of oral iron for children and adolescents with iron-deficiency anaemia [14], and another 2025 meta-analysis examined psychiatric and cognitive outcomes of iron in people who are iron deficient but not anaemic, such as menstruating adults [4]. A review of dietary heme iron discusses its efficacy and tolerability [15].

No randomised trial of iron supplementation for hair growth or other cosmetic outcomes appears in the research record for this entry. The clinical literature concerns iron deficiency and anaemia in general medical settings.

Meta-analyses and trials include: oral ferrous bisglycinate versus other iron preparations [8][9]; oral dose and duration in paediatric anaemia [14]; intravenous versus oral iron in pregnancy [12][13]; intravenous iron in heart failure with iron deficiency [7]; infection risk associated with intravenous iron compared with oral iron or none [16]; the relationship between iron deficiency and thyroid function [3]; cognitive and psychiatric outcomes in non-anaemic iron deficiency [4]; and the effect of iron on the infant gut microbiome in a Bangladeshi randomised trial [17]. An older randomised trial examined oral iron tolerance [18].

Registered trials include studies of ferrous sulfate versus iron amino acid chelate, sucrosomial iron in ulcerative colitis, intravenous versus oral iron in haemodialysis and inflammatory bowel disease, and iron absorption after gastric bypass [19][20][21][22][23].

Oral iron commonly causes gastrointestinal effects such as nausea, constipation, diarrhoea and heartburn; US product labelling describes these as usually mild, notes that taking iron with meals or reducing the dose may lessen them, and states that dark stools are a harmless result of unabsorbed iron [5]. Tolerability has been the motivation for newer formulations such as ferrous bisglycinate, which trials and a meta-analysis have compared with iron salts for gastrointestinal events [8][9]. A randomised study of oral iron tolerance appeared as early as 1974 [18].

Accidental overdose of iron-containing products is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under six, and labels carry a prominent warning to keep products out of children's reach [5]. Excess body iron is toxic through oxidative stress and tissue damage, as seen in haemochromatosis [1]; iron-dependent cell death, termed ferroptosis, is a separate subject of laboratory research [24][25]. A 2021 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined infection risk with intravenous iron versus oral iron or no iron [16]. Because anaemia can have causes other than iron deficiency, product labels note that it requires investigation to determine its cause [5].

Iron is a component of haemoglobin, which carries oxygen, and of enzymes involved in cellular respiration and DNA synthesis [1]. Its absorption is regulated by hepcidin, a hormone discussed in a 2023 review of iron in health and disease [11]; oral iron doses raise hepcidin and reduce absorption of subsequent doses [10]. The proposed link to hair is that follicle cells have high iron demand, and low stores may push follicles prematurely into telogen; this is a physiological hypothesis rather than a result established in hair-specific trials.

Elemental iron has atomic number 26 and exists mainly as iron(II) and iron(III) in compounds [2][1]. Supplements use ferrous salts, chelates and polysaccharide complexes with differing tolerability and bioavailability profiles [8].

Iron deficiency is a major global burden; Global Burden of Disease analyses list it among leading causes of years lived with disability [26][27], and an estimated 1.9 billion people worldwide had anaemia as of 2021, according to one summary [1]. In bodybuilding and physique forums, iron appears occasionally in blood-test threads, often alongside advice that markers be checked before supplements are started. Forum posts on the subject in the research record are sparse, and no distinct looksmaxxing protocol centred on iron is documented here.
